_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Botswana covering San/Bushmen (oldest continuous inhabitants), Tswana kingdoms, Bechuanaland protectorate, Seretse Khama interracial marriage controversy, independence 1966, diamond economy (Debswana), and Africa's democratic success story with highest HDI growth.

ethnic_groups.name: Tswana
ethnic_groups.notes: Dominant ethnic group comprising multiple sub-groups (see below); Setswana language

ethnic_groups.name: Bangwato
ethnic_groups.notes: Largest Tswana subgroup; Seretse Khama's royal house; central district

ethnic_groups.name: Bakwena
ethnic_groups.notes: Traditional royal group; associated with Molepolole; Livingstone's hosts

ethnic_groups.name: Kalanga
ethnic_groups.notes: Second-largest group; northeastern Botswana; related to Shona; historically linked to Butua/Rozvi states

ethnic_groups.name: San/Basarwa
ethnic_groups.notes: Indigenous hunter-gatherers; Kalahari; multiple groups (Gǀui, Gǁana, ǂHoan, !Kung); marginalised; land rights controversies

ethnic_groups.name: Herero
ethnic_groups.notes: Arrived from Namibia after German genocide; cattle pastoralists in Ngamiland/Ghanzi

ethnic_groups.name: Kgalagadi
ethnic_groups.notes: Kalahari region; culturally affiliated with Tswana but historically subordinate

ethnic_groups.name: Mbukushu
ethnic_groups.notes: Okavango Delta; fishing and farming communities

natural_resources.notes: World's largest diamond producer by value (Debswana 50/50 with De Beers); Orapa/Jwaneng mines among world's richest; rare 'African miracle'—used diamond wealth for development not corruption; also world's largest known coal deposits (largely unexploited due to landlocked geography/climate commitments)
natural_resources.resource_curse_risk: Low (transparent diamond revenue management, Pula Fund)

military.notes: Botswana Defence Force (BDF) well-trained; anti-poaching units (shoot-to-kill policy for rhino poachers); has never fought a foreign war; British/US military training

infrastructure.notes: Landlocked — fibre via South Africa and Namibia; Trans-Kalahari Highway; Kazungula Bridge (2021); BotswanaFibre Networks; Masama/BOFINET backbone.

climate_environment.notes: Okavango Delta threatened by water extraction upstream (Namibia/Angola); Kalahari desertification; large elephant population management challenge; world's richest diamond biodiversity.

debt_aid.notes: Graduated from least developed country (LDC) to upper-middle-income in one generation; one of Africa's best fiscal managers; minimal foreign debt; no IMF program ever needed

top_universities: Botswana International University of Science and Technology (BIUST)
education.notes: Free primary education; high enrollment rates; HIV/AIDS impact on teacher workforce; government scholarship program sends students abroad; education expenditure ~8% of GDP (among highest globally)

diaspora_migration.notes: Net immigration country (workers from Zimbabwe/Zambia in diamond mines); small diaspora relative to population; xenophobia concerns toward Zimbabwean migrants
diaspora_migration.immigration_policy: Selective; work permits for skilled labour

digital_economy.notes: Government-backed Innovation Hub at Gaborone; De Beers blockchain diamond tracking (Tracr); fibre optic connectivity improving; e-government services expanding; aim to diversify beyond diamonds with tech sector

country_profile.notes_unique: Africa's longest continuous multi-party democracy since independence (1966); transformed from one of the poorest countries to upper-middle-income through diamond revenues.
country_profile.national_anthem: Fatshe leno la rona (This Land of Ours)

lowest_point.name: Confluence of Limpopo and Shashe Rivers

geography.terrain: Predominantly flat; Kalahari Desert (70%); Okavango Delta (northwest); Makgadikgadi salt pans
geography.notes: Okavango Delta (world's largest inland delta, UNESCO World Heritage); Kalahari semi-desert; Makgadikgadi Pans largest salt flats in world; four-country meeting point (with Zambia, Namibia, Zimbabwe) at Kazungula.

economy_extended.notes: Africa's development success story (poorest at independence 1966, now upper-middle income); diamond-driven growth (Debswana); transparent governance; Sovereign Wealth Fund (Pula Fund); diversification challenge; high inequality.

health.notes: One of the world's highest HIV prevalence rates; pioneering ARV treatment programme (Masa programme, 2002); life expectancy recovered from 43 (2002) to 69; National Health Insurance planned.

food_agriculture.notes: Cattle culturally and economically important; Beef Protocol (EU export quotas); Botswana Meat Commission; Kalahari limits agriculture; food imports mainly from South Africa.

energy.notes: Morupule A&B coal power stations; massive coal reserves (200+ billion tonnes); solar potential enormous (300+ sunny days/year); imports from Eskom (South Africa); 100MW solar farm at Lerala.

transport.notes: Trans-Kalahari Highway (connects to Namibia/Walvis Bay); Kazungula Bridge (2021, connecting to Zambia); landlocked—relies on road transport through South Africa for trade.

tourism.notes: High-value, low-volume tourism policy; Okavango Delta one of Africa's premier safari destinations; Chobe (largest elephant population in world); luxury wildlife lodges; Botswana Ecotourism Certification.

human_rights_gender.notes: One of Africa's most stable democracies; LGBT decriminalisation (2019 High Court ruling landmark); death penalty still applied (rare); San/Bushman land rights contentious.

security_stability.notes: One of Africa's most peaceful and stable nations; Botswana Defence Force professional and apolitical; no history of civil conflict or coups; anti-poaching operations.

cultural_heritage.film_industry: Small (The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency filmed here)
cultural_heritage.media_landscape: Relatively free press; Daily News (state), Mmegi, The Voice (private); BTV; private FM stations
cultural_heritage.notes: Setswana culture dominant; San/Bushman indigenous heritage; No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency novels (Alexander McCall Smith) set in Gaborone; Botswana one of world's diamond polishing centres.

legal_system.notes: Dual court system (civil/customary); Kgotla (traditional assembly) still resolves local disputes; High Court/Court of Appeal; SADC Tribunal previously in Gaborone; strong rule of law for Africa.

comparative_rankings._note: Country position relative to continent and global.
comparative_rankings.notes: Africa's governance and development success story; diamond wealth; strong institutions; high per-capita GDP.

current_leader.name: Duma Boko
current_leader.title: President
current_leader.notes: Umbrella for Democratic Change (UDC) leader; first non-BDP president in Botswana's history

former_leaders.name: Seretse Khama
former_leaders.notes: Founding president; BDP leader; diamond economy architect; died in office

former_leaders.name: Quett Masire
former_leaders.notes: Continued prudent governance; economic growth; peacefully retired

former_leaders.name: Festus Mogae
former_leaders.notes: Managed HIV/AIDS crisis; Mo Ibrahim Prize winner; peacefully retired

former_leaders.name: Ian Khama
former_leaders.notes: Son of Seretse Khama; conservation focus; later split from BDP

former_leaders.name: Mokgweetsi Masisi
former_leaders.notes: Lost 2024 election; first BDP president to lose power

910.name: San/Bushmen – Oldest Continuous Inhabitants
910.description: The San (Bushmen) are among the world's oldest continuous populations, with deep archaeological and genetic roots in the Kalahari and broader southern Africa.

sub_clusters.name: Early and Middle Stone Age Occupation
sub_clusters.description: Stone tool sites across Botswana, including Tsodilo Hills, indicate continuous human occupation for over 100,000 years.

sub_clusters.name: Tsodilo Hills Rock Art
sub_clusters.description: UNESCO World Heritage site with over 4,500 rock paintings; 'Louvre of the Desert'; sacred to the San and later Bantu-speaking peoples.

sub_clusters.name: San Hunter-Gatherer Society
sub_clusters.description: Sophisticated knowledge of Kalahari ecology; trance healing dances; egalitarian social organisation; click languages of Khoisan family.

920.name: Bantu Migration and Rise of Tswana Kingdoms
920.description: Bantu-speaking peoples migrate into the region, introducing pastoralism, agriculture, and iron-working; Tswana chiefdoms begin to form.

sub_clusters.name: Bantu Migration into Botswana
sub_clusters.description: Iron Age Bantu-speaking farmers settle in eastern Botswana; cattle pastoralism becomes central to social organisation.

sub_clusters.name: Toutswe Tradition and Early States
sub_clusters.description: Toutswe hilltop settlements in eastern Botswana; cattle-based hierarchy; trade links with Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe.

sub_clusters.name: Formation of Tswana Chiefdoms
sub_clusters.description: Tswana-speaking groups (Bakwena, Bangwaketse, Bangwato, Batawana) emerge as distinct polities with centralised leadership under kgosi (chief).

930.name: Tswana Kingdoms and the Difaqane
930.description: Tswana kingdoms consolidate and expand; the Difaqane/Mfecane disruptions reshape the political landscape of the region.

sub_clusters.name: Tswana Political System and Kgotla
sub_clusters.description: Tswana governance through kgotla (public assembly); bogosi (chieftainship) traditions; cattle as wealth and status; large towns like Dithakong.

sub_clusters.name: Difaqane/Mfecane Impact on Botswana
sub_clusters.description: Zulu expansion and Ndebele raids under Mzilikazi devastate Tswana communities; massive population displacement and political reconfiguration.

940.name: European Contact and Bechuanaland Protectorate
940.description: Missionary influence, Boer encroachment, and the establishment of British Bechuanaland Protectorate; Tswana chiefs' diplomacy preserves autonomy.

sub_clusters.name: Missionaries and David Livingstone
sub_clusters.description: Robert Moffat and David Livingstone establish missions among the Bakwena; Livingstone marries Mary Moffat at Kuruman; Christianity and literacy spread.

sub_clusters.name: Three Chiefs' Petition to London 1895
sub_clusters.description: Chiefs Khama III, Bathoen I, and Sebele I travel to London in 1895 to prevent Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company from absorbing Bechuanaland; protectorate preserved.

sub_clusters.name: Bechuanaland Protectorate Administration
sub_clusters.description: Minimal British administration governed from Mafikeng (outside the territory); indirect rule through Tswana chiefs; deliberate underdevelopment; resistance to incorporation into South Africa.

940.name: Seretse Khama Interracial Marriage Controversy
940.description: Seretse Khama's marriage to Englishwoman Ruth Williams triggers an international scandal driven by apartheid South Africa's pressure on Britain.

sub_clusters.name: Seretse Khama–Ruth Williams Marriage
sub_clusters.description: Seretse Khama, heir to the Bangwato chieftainship, marries Ruth Williams in London 1948; apartheid South Africa and the Bangwato regent oppose the union.

sub_clusters.name: British Exile of Seretse Khama
sub_clusters.description: Britain exiles Seretse to appease apartheid South Africa and protect uranium supplies; international outcry; Seretse renounces chieftainship to return in 1956.

950.name: Independence and Nation Building
950.description: Seretse Khama leads Botswana to independence in 1966; founds Botswana Democratic Party; discovery of diamonds transforms one of the world's poorest countries.

sub_clusters.name: Botswana Democratic Party and Independence
sub_clusters.description: Seretse Khama founds BDP 1962; leads Bechuanaland to independence on 30 September 1966; becomes first president of Botswana.

sub_clusters.name: Diamond Discovery at Orapa
sub_clusters.description: Discovery of Orapa diamond pipe 1967; Jwaneng (richest mine by value) found 1972; Debswana partnership (50/50 with De Beers) established.

sub_clusters.name: Seretse Khama's Presidency
sub_clusters.description: Prudent management of diamond revenues; investment in education and infrastructure; multiparty democracy maintained; Seretse dies in office 1980.

960.name: Botswana: Africa's Democratic Success Story
960.description: Botswana achieves highest sustained economic growth in the world; stable multiparty democracy; highest HDI growth rate in Africa; navigates HIV/AIDS crisis and economic diversification.

sub_clusters.name: Masire and Mogae Presidencies
sub_clusters.description: Quett Masire (1980–1998) and Festus Mogae (1998–2008) continue prudent governance; Pula Fund sovereign wealth management; anti-corruption institutions.

sub_clusters.name: HIV/AIDS Crisis and Response
sub_clusters.description: Botswana hit by one of the world's highest HIV prevalence rates (nearly 40% at peak); pioneering free antiretroviral treatment program under Mogae.

sub_clusters.name: Economic Diversification and Diamond Dependence
sub_clusters.description: Efforts to diversify beyond diamonds into tourism (Okavango Delta UNESCO site), financial services, and beef exports; De Beers moves aggregation to Gaborone.

sub_clusters.name: 2024 Democratic Transition
sub_clusters.description: President Mokgweetsi Masisi and BDP face increasing opposition; first-ever transfer of power from BDP to opposition in 2024 elections; deepening of democratic norms.

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
